text:
Customer John: Hey team — since we flipped the new gateway policy this morning we're seeing a flood of 429s from the private gateway and p99 latency spikes. First spike at ~08:10, now it's persistent. Customer-side rate limits should be pretty conservative, not sure why they're exhausted so fast. example curl: `curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer ..." https://gateway.customer-vpc.example/v1/generate` returns 429 with `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0` and `x-request-id` logs show a lot of backpressure.
Ava (Support): Thanks John — sorry about the hit. Can you confirm whether you recently changed the ingress controller (nginx -> envoy) or added a global token-bucket policy on the gateway? Any recent bursts from batch jobs or cron workers? Also, what's your normal QPS vs the observed burst?
Customer John: We did roll out a change to the envoy config for better TLS handling yesterday. Normal steady QPS ~50, but during the job window we hit ~650 for ~30s. We expected rate limiter to allow short bursts; behavior looks like limiter dropped many connections instead of smoothing.
Eli (Eng-Infra): Sounds like classic burst vs quota exhaustion mismatch. Two things to check: (1) per-connection concurrency / connection_pool settings, (2) token bucket burst size and refill rate in Envoy.Filter.RateLimit or in your kube ingress annotations. If the bucket capacity is too small, a short 600qps spike will immediately exhaust tokens and then you'll see prolonged tail because of retry storms.
Priya (Oncall): Can you paste the gateway rate limit snippet? Common problematic config we see:
```
envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit:
  stat_prefix: http_local_rate_limiter
  token_bucket:
    max_tokens: 100
    tokens_per_fill: 1
    fill_interval: 1s
```
That config has too low max_tokens for your burst. For a short 30s spike you want something like `max_tokens: 1200` or use a higher tokens_per_fill to smooth over 1-5s windows.
Customer John: Here's what we have in the k8s annotation on the customer gateway service:
`service.beta.kubernetes.io/envoy-rate-limit: "token=100;rate=1/s;burst=200"` — maybe that burst=200 is applied per-pod, and we scaled to 3 pods during the rollout which changed effective capacity unexpectedly.
Ava (Support): Exactly — per-pod semantics often confuse customers. If the limit is per-pod, total cluster bursting = pods * burst. But if autoscaler lag or proxy restarts create uneven distribution, you can hit a single pod hot-spot. Also watch for client-side connection reuse: if clients open many concurrent connections and one pod receives disproportionate traffic, its token bucket drains faster.
Eli (Eng-Infra): Short repro you can run (safe non-prod): a small loop to hammer at 600 qps for 20s to reproduce the 429 tail. Example using vegeta or simple curl loop with parallel jobs. If you want me to run something from our end we'll coordinate windows.
Customer John: We can run a repro in staging — do you have recommended tuning? Prefer minimal changes to avoid breaking other assumptions.
Priya (Oncall): Minimal safe changes:
- Increase max_tokens (bucket capacity) to allow a 30s worth of expected burst: e.g., max_tokens = expected_peak_qps * burst_window_seconds (650 * 30 ~ 19500) but you can be conservative and start with 2000-5000.
- Increase fill rate to match sustained QPS (e.g., tokens_per_fill: 50 / fill_interval: 1s for 50 qps steady).
- Add jittered client backoff and small retries on 429s (idempotent requests only) — prevents retry storms.
- Add metrics: per-pod `local_rate_limit.allowed` / `local_rate_limit.enforced` counters and histogram of `x-envoy-upstream-rq-time`, and surface a dashboard.
Sven (Customer Success): If you need immediate relief, consider enabling a soft fallback route to a lower-cost, higher-concurrency model or temporarily increasing Dedicated pool capacity, if you have Dedicated. That avoids user-visible failures while we tune configs.
Eli (Eng-Infra): Also check K8s Service and Ingress settings: some ingress controllers have connection limits (worker_connections) and default proxy buffers. Example NGINX annotation to allow more connections:
`nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/limit-connections: "2000"`
and for Envoy you might want to tune `per_connection_buffer_limit_bytes` and `connection_pool` settings in the upstream cluster config.
Customer John: We saw a pattern where after the initial 429s the client retries in bursts and then we see a long tail of degraded latency even after inbound qps drops — I assume that's retry amplification.
Ava (Support): Yes — typical. Two mitigation threads:
1) Fail fast non-critical requests client-side (circuit-breakers).
2) Add a short randomized retry jitter and exponential backoff server-side.
Also consider changing limiter semantics from strict reject to queue with short max wait (if your gateway supports it) — that'll smooth spikes but increases p99 latency.
Priya (Oncall): Quick commands to inspect remaining tokens and tokens refill (if metrics enabled):
```
kubectl -n gateway logs deploy/envoy-gw -c envoy --tail 200 | grep local_rate_limit
# or query /stats endpoint on envoy: curl http://envoy-admin:9901/stats | grep local_rate_limit
```
Customer John: We pulled admin stats and saw `http_local_rate_limiter.allowed = 120` and `http_local_rate_limiter.enforced = 540` — means many enforcement events.
Eli (Eng-Infra): Plan of action:
- In staging: bump token bucket max_tokens to 4000 and tokens_per_fill to 50/s. Run a controlled 600 qps spike for 30s and collect metrics.
- If staging OK, roll to prod with canary on 10% of pods, watch `local_rate_limit.enforced` and p99.
- Add client retry jitter and update docs for per-pod vs cluster semantics.
Customer John: Ok we'll test staging now. One last thing — billing/quotas: will these 429s count as consumed tokens and potentially hit upstream billing quota on Redwood API? We saw a spike on our consumption billing yesterday.
Ava (Support): Good question — 429s are rejected at the gateway so they shouldn't count as completed token usage for model tokens, but if requests are forwarded before rate check or the gateway retries automatically, that can generate model calls. Ensure gateway rejects early (local rate limit should reject before any upstream call). We'll double-check gateway logs for any forwarded requests that returned 429s upstream.
Priya (Oncall): I'll run a short audit: check request logs for `upstream_response_time` and `upstream_attempts` and confirm whether those 429s hit Redwood backend. If they did we'll coordinate with billing to adjust or annotate the spike.
ops-bot: Incident created: INC-2026-0423-78 — assigned to Eli, Priya, Ava. Slack thread linked.
Customer John: Thanks all — running staging repro now. Will post results and admin stats.
Ava (Support): Ping us if you see enforcement drop but p99 still high; we can help tune queueing vs rejecting. Also happy to schedule a short runbook session to walk through tuning and metric dashboards.
Customer John: Repro in staging: with max_tokens=4000 we still see 429s but enforcement dropped from 540->60 and latency p99 reduced from 2.4s -> 0.9s. Looks much better. We'll proceed with canary.
Eli (Eng-Infra): Great. After canary, add an annotation in your deployment notes about per-pod semantics and include the script you used for repro so future deploys test the limiter. Also consider adding a small global token bucket on top of per-pod to avoid single-pod hot spot if feasible.
Customer John: Will do. Thanks team! :thumbsup:
